newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms raise funds through debt placements.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms raise funds through debt placements.

text.p: Indian firms are raising funds through private placements of debt in a big way, marking a shift from the traditional means of funding through bank loans, bankers and analysts said on Wednesday.
"It's the flavour of the season," said one bank treasurer.
"It's a very neat, clean and fast way to raise funds," said Arun Bhatnagar, deputy manager (private placements) at SBI Capital Markets Ltd, a leading merchant bank.
Research firm PRIME Database said private debt placements rose 82 percent in 1996/97 (April-March), with 204 issues raising 181.04 billion rupees.
Private placements and commercial paper (CP) continue to be favourites in the new fiscal year which began in April 1997.
Company treasurers say the phenomenon reflects the emergence of a new breed of institutional players in the market.

"We have large mutual funds and asset management companies with money," said K. Sridharan, deputy general manager (corporate finance) at truck maker Ashok Leyland Ltd. "We are trying to leverage them."
Ashok Leyland is raising 2.0 billion rupees through a private placement.
Other attractions of private placements include a smaller client base and more efficient pricing, he said.
Interaction with prospective subscribers provides an insight into what the market can bear, unlike in a retail public issue.
"In this case, we sensed the strength (of our issue) and lowered the coupon to 14.0 percent (a year)," Sridharan said.
India's public sector banks, which dominate the industry, have been under pressure to boost profits since most plan to raise capital through public issues of shares later this year.
"These debt issues are more liquid than loans -- they are tradable," said one banker.
Top-rated firms can raise funds through private placements at rates very close to public sector banks' prime lending rate of 13.5 percent and commercial papers at 8.5-10.0 percent.
Investments in debt by rated companies save banks several of the procedural hassles which come with bank loans.

One is that there is no capital adequacy requirement for investment in bonds. Another advantage is loans are made against hypothecation of assets requiring periodic inspection by bank personnel while there are no such requirements for debt.
The latest Reserve Bank of India (RBI) figures show total bank deposits at 5,214.42 billion rupees on July 4, 1997, an increase of 775.89 billion over the year-ago figure.
Bank advances, however, grew by only 243.68 billion rupees in the same period, to 2,774.60 billion.
Analysts said the falling rate of bank advances only partly reflected a slowdown in Indian industry as RBI statistics represent only bank loans.
Bankers said the days when companies made a beeline for banks seeking loans may be drawing to a close.

"Those days are over. Top-rated clients will have a basket of options to choose from," said K.S. Sridhar, head of credit at ABN-AMRO Bank N.V. in Bombay, referring to the popularity of bonds, commercial paper and external commercial borrowings.
